newsitem.title: USA: AMR remains committed to Canadian Airlines.
newsitem.headline: AMR remains committed to Canadian Airlines.

text.p: AMR Corp said on Friday it remains committed to its stake in Canadian Airlines International but does not plan any further investment in the ailing carrier.
Earlier today Canadian Airlines released year-to-date financial results that were much worse than expected.
Canadian Airlines, which could face a cash crunch in the first quarter of 1997, said that to stem its losses, it would seek wage cuts from employees and concessions from AMR.
AMR, the parent of American Airlines, said it would consider "all reasonable Canadian requests for additional assistance."

AMR said it had confidence in Canadian Air's new management team and would wait to see the company's final plan before determining whether "further financial participation by AMR makes business sense."
"If an additional cash infusion by AMR would have ensured Canadian's long-term profitability, we would have given such an investment strong consideration," AMR said.
"The reality, however, is that both Canadian and Air Canada have been doing poorly in a Canadian airline environment marked by substantial excess capacity."
It continued, "Canadian Airlines's own situation is complicated by the fact it has inadequate liquidity."
AMR previously said it might post a charge against 1996 earnings for the decline in market value of its investment in Canadian Air.
It originally invested $177 million in Canadian Air in 1994. The market value of that investment grew to $192 million with dividends, but has now declined to $32 million, the company said.
AMR holds a one-third economic interest in Canadian Air and a 25 percent voting interest.

The two airlines have a code-sharing and marketing alliance. AMR also collects about $100 million annually from Canadian Air by providing reservation services, computer and management information services.
